text: [TRUE] The carriageway shown is two-way with two lanes per direction; overtaking (sorpasso) does not invade the opposite lane, so it is allowed even on a curve.
[TRUE] The double continuous white line in the middle separates the two directions of travel, so the carriageway is two-way (doppio senso di circolazione).
[TRUE] On this type of extra-urban carriageway the outer (right) lane is for ordinary driving, while the inner lanes are, as a rule, reserved for overtaking (sorpasso).
[TRUE] The central double continuous white line may never be crossed, so making a U-turn (inversione di marcia) is prohibited.
[FALSE] Overtaking is normally done on the left; passing on the right is allowed only in special cases (e.g. the vehicle ahead is turning left), not indifferently from both sides.
[FALSE] Driving in parallel columns (marcia per file parallele) is generally prohibited; vehicles must proceed in single file within their lane, so it is not 'always' possible.
[FALSE] You must not begin an overtaking manoeuvre if the driver behind has already started the same manoeuvre (sorpasso), to avoid several vehicles driving abreast.
[TRUE] On a road with three lanes per direction, the right (outermost) lane is, as a rule, for ordinary driving (marcia ordinaria), leaving the others for overtaking.
[TRUE] The road shown is a single two-way carriageway with three lanes on each side of the central double continuous line, i.e. three lanes per direction.
[TRUE] On this type of road the right lane is for ordinary driving, while the centre and left lanes are, as a rule, reserved for overtaking (sorpasso).
[TRUE] There is no median (spartitraffico), only a double continuous line separating the directions, so the road consists of a single carriageway (carreggiata).
[FALSE] The centre lane is, as a rule, reserved for overtaking (sorpasso); ordinary driving belongs in the right-hand lane.
[FALSE] The right-hand lane is for ordinary driving (marcia ordinaria); overtaking is done using the centre and left lanes.
[FALSE] The left-hand lane is, as a rule, reserved for overtaking (sorpasso); ordinary driving belongs in the right-hand lane.
[TRUE] The two medians (spartitraffico, shown as green lines) divide the road into three carriageways: two lateral ones plus the central one.
[TRUE] The road has eight lanes (corsie) in total: four on the central two-way carriageway and two on each lateral one-way carriageway.
[TRUE] The lateral carriageways, separated from each other by medians and the central carriageway, are, as a rule, one-way (senso unico).
[TRUE] The central carriageway has no physical separation inside, so it is, as a rule, two-way (doppio senso di circolazione).
[TRUE] Since each direction has its own lanes, overtaking (sorpasso) does not invade oncoming traffic, so it is allowed even on a bend.
[FALSE] The road has three carriageways, not four, and the central one is two-way, so they are not all one-way.
[FALSE] The road has three carriageways (carreggiate) and eight lanes (corsie); do not confuse lanes with carriageways.
[FALSE] Only the central carriageway is, as a rule, two-way; the two lateral carriageways are one-way.
[FALSE] The road has eight lanes (corsie); three is the number of carriageways, not of lanes.
[FALSE] The lateral carriageways are one-way and the medians (spartitraffico) may not be crossed, so making a U-turn (inversione di marcia) is prohibited.
[TRUE] A pedestrian crossing (attraversamento pedonale) is marked by a set of parallel white stripes painted on the carriageway.
[TRUE] A pedestrian crossing is part of the carriageway (carreggiata) on which even stopping (fermata) is prohibited, so as not to obstruct pedestrians.
[TRUE] Pedestrians crossing on the stripes have right of way (precedenza) and vehicles must yield to them.
[TRUE] The pedestrian crossing is the part of the carriageway intended for pedestrians who are crossing.
[TRUE] Parking (sosta) on a pedestrian crossing is prohibited, and stopping (fermata) is forbidden as well.
[FALSE] The crossing consists of white stripes painted on the carriageway itself; it is not a part of the road separated from the carriageway by a yellow stripe.
[FALSE] Vehicle transit over the crossing is not forbidden — vehicles may drive across it but must yield to pedestrians on the stripes; what is prohibited is stopping and parking.
[FALSE] The pedestrian crossing is precisely part of the carriageway (carreggiata).
[FALSE] The crossing lies on the carriageway, not outside it; pedestrian areas outside the carriageway are sidewalks (marciapiede) and shoulders (banchina).
[FALSE] On a pedestrian crossing both stopping (fermata) and parking (sosta) are prohibited, not only parking.
[TRUE] Main extra-urban roads (strade extraurbane principali) have independent carriageways, or carriageways separated by a median (spartitraffico).
[TRUE] Like motorways, main extra-urban roads are equipped with dedicated parking areas (aree di sosta) along the route.
[TRUE] Main extra-urban roads have no at-grade crossings (incroci a raso); all intersections are grade-separated for safety and speed.
[TRUE] Main extra-urban roads are marked by dedicated start and end signs (blue background).
[TRUE] Only certain categories of motor vehicles may use main extra-urban roads; bicycles, mopeds (ciclomotori) and light quadricycles are excluded.
[TRUE] Since at-grade crossings are excluded, intersections on main extra-urban roads are grade-separated (intersezioni a livelli sfalsati).
[TRUE] Main extra-urban roads are entered via acceleration lanes (corsia di accelerazione) and left via deceleration lanes.
[FALSE] The maximum speed on main extra-urban roads is 110 km/h; 130 km/h applies to motorways (autostrade).
[FALSE] Main extra-urban roads have blue signage; green signs (segnaletica verde) identify motorways.
[FALSE] The speed limit on main extra-urban roads is 110 km/h, lower than the 130 km/h allowed on motorways.
[FALSE] Light quadricycles (quadricicli leggeri), like mopeds, are banned from main extra-urban roads.
[FALSE] Main extra-urban roads have at least two lanes per direction, not just one.
[FALSE] Mopeds (ciclomotori) may not travel on main extra-urban roads.
[FALSE] The law does not require main extra-urban roads to be free of curves or humps; their defining features are separated carriageways, no at-grade crossings and dedicated entry/exit lanes.
[TRUE] The main function of a traffic island (isola di traffico) is to separate and channel traffic flows towards their various directions.
[TRUE] A traffic island is delimited by continuous white stripes, which must not be crossed.
[TRUE] A traffic island may be at grade (a raso, painted with white hatching) or raised (rialzata).
[TRUE] Traffic islands (especially at-grade ones) are highlighted by white hatching (zebrature), signalling that vehicles must keep off.
[TRUE] All vehicle transit is prohibited on a traffic island, including motorcycles (motocicli).
[TRUE] An at-grade (a raso) traffic island consists exactly of the white hatching painted on the road surface.
[TRUE] A raised traffic island is preceded by white hatching (zebrature) that guides vehicles around the obstacle in advance.
[TRUE] The traffic island is a part of the road closed to vehicle transit, parking and stopping; it serves to separate and channel traffic flows.
[FALSE] A traffic island separates and channels traffic flows; the carriageway is separated from the shoulder (banchina) by the continuous edge line, not by an island.
[FALSE] The traffic island is closed to vehicles and not intended for pedestrians; the refuge for crossing pedestrians is the salvagente.
[FALSE] Transit and parking are forbidden on a traffic island; a parking lay-by (piazzola di sosta) is a separate area off the carriageway.
[FALSE] No vehicle may drive over a traffic island — taxis and urban buses included.
[FALSE] A traffic island is a marked or raised area of the road used to channel traffic; it has nothing to do with how busy a city district is.
[FALSE] A traffic island has nothing to do with the historic centre (centro storico); it is a road channelling device.
[FALSE] Vehicles may not enter a traffic island, so it cannot be used to make a U-turn (inversione di marcia).
[FALSE] The traffic island is part of the road (strada), located on the carriageway surface itself.
[FALSE] Both stopping (fermata) and parking (sosta) are prohibited on a traffic island.
[FALSE] It is the pedestrian refuge (salvagente), not the traffic island, that facilitates boarding and alighting from trams, trolleybuses and buses.
[FALSE] Vehicles may neither enter nor park on a traffic island; it is by no means a parking area.
[FALSE] An urban pedestrian area (area pedonale) is reserved for pedestrians; a traffic island sits on the carriageway and is closed to vehicles without being a pedestrian area.
[FALSE] All vehicles, mopeds (ciclomotori) included, are prohibited from travelling on a traffic island.
[TRUE] A grade-separated intersection (intersezione a livelli sfalsati) is defined by the intersecting roads being located at different heights.
[TRUE] Grade-separated intersections ease traffic flow and improve safety by eliminating direct crossing points between vehicles; they are used on motorways, for example.
[TRUE] Grade-separated intersections connect roads at different levels by means of ramps (rampe), overpasses (sovrappassi) and underpasses (sottopassi).
[TRUE] Grade-separated intersections are equipped with infrastructure — ramps, overpasses, underpasses — linking roads situated at different levels.
[FALSE] An at-grade crossing between a road and railway tracks is a level crossing (passaggio a livello); a grade-separated intersection involves roads at different heights.
[FALSE] The general maximum speed limits apply also within grade-separated intersections; drivers must still respect them.
[FALSE] Grade-separated intersections have no direct crossing points, so traffic lights are normally unnecessary; traffic lights (semafori) regulate at-grade intersections.
[TRUE] An at-grade intersection (intersezione a raso) is where two or more roads cross at the same level.
[TRUE] An at-grade intersection may be regulated by traffic lights (semaforo) or governed by right-of-way rules.
[TRUE] This is the very definition of an at-grade intersection: two or more roads at the same level crossing each other — the most common type in towns.
[TRUE] At an at-grade intersection traffic flows meet directly, so special attention to vehicles coming from the crossing roads is required to avoid accidents.
[FALSE] An at-grade intersection is a crossing of two or more roads at the same level; tram tracks (binari del tram) have nothing to do with the definition.
[FALSE] A driveway access (passo carrabile) is an access from the public road to a private area, not an intersection between roads.
[FALSE] A crossing equipped with barriers or half-barriers is a level crossing (passaggio a livello) between a road and a railway, not an at-grade intersection between roads.
[FALSE] The two are opposites: at-grade intersections (a raso) are on the same level, grade-separated ones (a livelli sfalsati) are at different levels.
[FALSE] A set of overpasses, underpasses and ramps characterises grade-separated intersections (a livelli sfalsati), not at-grade ones.
[TRUE] A limited traffic zone (zona a traffico limitato, ZTL) may restrict vehicle circulation only during certain time slots (fasce orarie).
[TRUE] A ZTL may limit circulation only to particular categories of vehicles (e.g. lorries, non-residents' vehicles).
[TRUE] In a ZTL only authorised (autorizzati) vehicles may circulate during the restricted hours.
[TRUE] The restriction may also apply only to particular categories of users (utenti), e.g. access reserved for residents or delivery operators.
[TRUE] A ZTL is delimited by dedicated start and end road signs (segnali di inizio e di fine).
[FALSE] A ZTL restricts vehicle categories, user categories or time slots — not the absolute number of vehicles that may enter.
[FALSE] A ZTL is not reserved for mopeds and bicycles; during restricted hours authorised vehicles — including cars — may enter.
[FALSE] A ZTL is not always closed to motor vehicles: the restriction applies only during set hours or to set categories of vehicles/users.
[FALSE] A ZTL restricts vehicle circulation; pedestrian access is never affected, and there is no night-time ban on pedestrians.
[TRUE] A level crossing (passaggio a livello) may have full barriers (barriere) that close the entire crossing when a train approaches.
[TRUE] Level crossings often have half-barriers (semibarriere) that close only the entry side of each direction.
[TRUE] Level crossings are equipped with flashing red lights (luci rosse) warning of an approaching train; transit is then forbidden.
[TRUE] Approaching a level crossing, distance marker panels (pannelli distanziometrici) with three, two and one red stripes announce 300, 200 and 100 metres to go.
[TRUE] The St. Andrew's cross (croce di S. Andrea) is placed right at the level crossing, marking the at-grade crossing between road and railway.
[TRUE] A level crossing may have an acoustic signalling device (segnalazione acustica) sounding a bell or alarm when a train approaches.
[FALSE] A level crossing is an at-grade crossing between road and railway; an overpass (cavalcavia) exists precisely to avoid such crossings.
[FALSE] Level crossings use red lights (luci rosse), not flashing yellow ones.
[FALSE] A level crossing is an at-grade crossing between a road and a railway line (linea ferroviaria); motorways are irrelevant here.
[FALSE] Acceleration lanes (corsie di accelerazione) belong to motorway and main extra-urban road entrances, not to level crossings.
[FALSE] A driveway access (passo carrabile) leads to a private area; a level crossing is the at-grade crossing between a road and railway tracks.
[FALSE] A level crossing is by definition at grade (a raso); an underpass (sottopassaggio) belongs to grade-separated solutions.
[TRUE] A pedestrian area (area pedonale) is in principle reserved for pedestrians, but zero-emission electric vehicles may enter if expressly allowed by an additional panel (pannello integrativo).
[TRUE] A pedestrian area (area pedonale) is by definition reserved for the transit of pedestrians.
[TRUE] Vehicles serving persons with disabilities (veicoli al servizio di persone diversamente abili) may enter pedestrian areas.
[TRUE] Police vehicles on emergency duty may enter pedestrian areas with siren and flashing blue light (sirena e lampeggiante blu) in operation.
[TRUE] Fire brigade vehicles on emergency duty, with flashing blue light and siren operating, may enter pedestrian areas.
[FALSE] Motorcycles (motocicli) may not enter pedestrian areas; only emergency vehicles, bicycles, vehicles serving disabled persons and vehicles expressly allowed by signs are admitted.
[FALSE] Road tractors (trattori stradali) may not travel in pedestrian areas, whatever their speed.
[FALSE] Mopeds (ciclomotori) are banned from pedestrian areas at all times; there is no daytime-only rule.
[FALSE] Ordinary motor vehicles (autoveicoli) are banned from pedestrian areas regardless of caution; only the exceptions listed by law may enter.
[FALSE] Motor quadricycles (quadricicli a motore) may not travel in pedestrian areas, regardless of speed.
[TRUE] A road (strada) may be divided by medians (spartitraffico) into several carriageways (carreggiate).
[TRUE] The road (strada) includes not only the carriageway but may also comprise cycle paths (piste ciclabili), sidewalks and shoulders.
[TRUE] A road may be one-way (senso unico), with all vehicles travelling in the same direction.
[TRUE] A road may also be two-way (doppio senso di circolazione), with vehicles travelling in both directions.
[TRUE] Under Art. 2 of the Highway Code, the road is a public-use area intended for the circulation of pedestrians, vehicles and animals.
[FALSE] The road (strada) does include the shoulders (banchine), as well as sidewalks and cycle paths; it is wider than the carriageway alone.
[FALSE] The road is open to pedestrians, animals and all kinds of vehicles including bicycles — not just cars and motorcycles.
[FALSE] 'Reserved for vehicles and animals only' describes the carriageway (carreggiata); the road (strada) also serves pedestrians and bicycles.
[FALSE] The road (strada) includes the sidewalks (marciapiedi), which are the part of the road outside the carriageway reserved for pedestrians.
[FALSE] The road is defined as a public-use area for pedestrians, vehicles and animals — not any paved area; pedestrian crossings are markings within the carriageway, not its lateral boundaries.
[TRUE] Motorways (autostrade) have no at-grade crossings (incroci a raso); all junctions are grade-separated to allow safe high-speed travel.
[TRUE] Motorways have acceleration lanes (corsia di accelerazione) for entering and deceleration lanes (corsia di decelerazione) for exiting.
[TRUE] Motorways consist of independent carriageways, or carriageways separated by a median (spartitraffico), and are fenced at the sides.
[TRUE] Only thermal-engine motorcycles below 120 cm³ are banned from motorways, so a 150 cm³ motorcycle (motociclo) may travel on them.
[TRUE] Agricultural machines (macchine agricole), being too slow, are expressly excluded from motorway circulation.
[TRUE] Not all vehicles may use motorways: vehicles unable to reach 80 km/h, mopeds, small-displacement motorcycles and agricultural machines are excluded.
[TRUE] Vehicles leave the motorway via deceleration lanes (corsia di decelerazione), slowing down only after leaving the main traffic flow.
[TRUE] Motorways must be fenced at the sides (recintate lateralmente) to keep out pedestrians and animals.
[FALSE] Motorcycles, lorries, buses and other motor vehicles may also use motorways — not only cars (autovetture).
[FALSE] Not all motorcycles may use motorways: those with thermal engines below 120 cm³ (or electric motors below 6 kW) are banned.
[FALSE] Motorways are reserved for eligible motor vehicles and cannot include cycle paths (piste ciclabili); bicycles are banned.
[FALSE] Mopeds (ciclomotori) are always banned from motorways, and thermal motorcycles must be at least 120 cm³ — so the claim about up to 125 cm³ is wrong.
[FALSE] Besides motor vehicles, motorcycles (motocicli) meeting the displacement requirement may also travel on motorways.
[FALSE] Mopeds (ciclomotori) and small-displacement motorcycles are excluded from motorways, so not all two-wheeled motor vehicles may circulate.
[TRUE] A carriageway (carreggiata) may be one-way (senso unico), like each side of a motorway.
[TRUE] A carriageway (carreggiata) may also be two-way (doppio senso), like the single carriageway of an ordinary two-way road.
[TRUE] A carriageway (carreggiata) may be divided into one or more lanes (corsie), each carrying a single file of vehicles.
[TRUE] Cycle paths (piste ciclabili) are not part of the carriageway; they are a separate part of the road (strada) running alongside it.
[TRUE] Sidewalks (marciapiedi) lie outside the carriageway; they belong to the road but not to the carriageway (carreggiata).
[TRUE] The carriageway (carreggiata) is the part of the road normally intended for the circulation of vehicles (and animals).
[FALSE] The carriageway serves all motor and non-motor vehicles and animals — not only animal-drawn carts.
[FALSE] The carriageway is for moving traffic, not emergency stopping; that belongs to the emergency lane (corsia di emergenza) or the shoulder.
[FALSE] The carriageway is intended for circulation, not parking; lorries should park in dedicated areas or lay-bys (piazzole di sosta).
[FALSE] The carriageway (carreggiata) is the part of the road intended for vehicle traffic; it has nothing to do with wheel tracks left in snow.
[FALSE] Parking lay-bys (piazzole di sosta) lie outside the carriageway and are not part of it (carreggiata).
[TRUE] Traffic lanes (corsie di marcia) are a basic component of the carriageway (carreggiata).
[TRUE] Cycle crossings (attraversamenti ciclabili) cut across the carriageway and are part of it — unlike cycle paths (pista ciclabile), which are not.
[TRUE] Pedestrian crossings (attraversamenti pedonali) are marked on the carriageway surface and form part of it (carreggiata).
[TRUE] Overtaking lanes (corsie di sorpasso), like traffic lanes, are part of the carriageway (carreggiata).
[FALSE] Shoulders (banchine) lie beyond the continuous edge line of the carriageway; they belong to the road but not to the carriageway (carreggiata).
[FALSE] Sidewalks (marciapiedi) are reserved for pedestrians, lie outside the carriageway, and are not part of it (carreggiata).
[TRUE] A lane (corsia) is part of the carriageway (carreggiata) and can be destined to the normal travel of vehicles.
[TRUE] A lane is delimited by continuous or discontinuous road markings, which indicate whether it may be crossed.
[TRUE] One type of lane is the acceleration lane (corsia di accelerazione), used to speed up before joining a motorway.
[TRUE] A lane can also be a deceleration lane (corsia di decelerazione), used to slow down when leaving a motorway.
[TRUE] Certain lanes may be closed to specific categories of vehicles by the road authority.
[TRUE] A lane can be reserved for certain vehicle categories, such as taxis or buses (corsia riservata).
[TRUE] A lane can be destined to overtaking (sorpasso), e.g. an overtaking lane.
[TRUE] The road owner may impose a mandatory minimum speed on a given lane (velocità minima obbligatoria).
[TRUE] By definition a lane is the part of the carriageway allowing the circulation of a single row of vehicles.
[TRUE] A lane can be destined to emergency stops (soste di emergenza), as with the emergency lane (corsia di emergenza).
[TRUE] A lane can be reserved for vehicles intending to turn: a specialised lane (corsia specializzata).
[TRUE] A lane can serve to slow down vehicles exiting motorways: the deceleration lane (corsia di decelerazione).
[FALSE] A lane is for vehicles, not only pedestrians; pedestrians use the pavement (marciapiede) or the shoulder (banchina).
[FALSE] A lane allows a single row of vehicles and can never be two-way (doppio senso).
[FALSE] A lane is simply a part of the carriageway; it has nothing to do with racing tracks.
[FALSE] Pedestrians can cross lanes at pedestrian crossings (attraversamenti pedonali), which are part of the carriageway.
[FALSE] A lane is part of a carriageway (carreggiata), not made of two carriageways — the relationship is the opposite.
[FALSE] A fast-flow road (strada a scorrimento veloce) is a class of road; a lane is only a part of a carriageway.
[FALSE] Even in built-up areas two motorcycles may not ride side by side in the same lane, which allows only one row of vehicles.
[FALSE] Two mopeds (ciclomotori) may never ride side by side in the same lane, inside or outside built-up areas.
[TRUE] The acceleration lane (corsia di accelerazione) eases entry onto motorways and main extra-urban roads by letting vehicles match the speed of the traffic flow.
[TRUE] The acceleration lane exists precisely to let vehicles enter a motorway correctly without hindering traffic.
[TRUE] The acceleration lane is used to increase speed so that merging does not obstruct other vehicles.
[TRUE] Acceleration lanes are also found at service-area exits, helping vehicles rejoin the motorway carriageway.
[FALSE] Overtaking (sorpasso) and stopping are forbidden on acceleration lanes, which serve only to gain speed and merge.
[FALSE] Acceleration lanes are never located at lay-bys (piazzole di sosta); they serve motorway and service-area entries.
[FALSE] Leaving the carriageway for a rest area is done via the deceleration lane (corsia di decelerazione), not the acceleration lane.
[TRUE] The deceleration lane (corsia di decelerazione) lets vehicles slow down before leaving a motorway, easing the exit.
[TRUE] The deceleration lane is used to exit main extra-urban roads correctly.
[TRUE] Deceleration lanes are generally at service-area entrances, allowing vehicles to slow down safely.
[FALSE] Stopping (sosta) is forbidden on deceleration lanes; they serve only to slow down before exiting.
[FALSE] Deceleration lanes are never at lay-bys (piazzole di sosta); they serve motorway exits and service areas.
[FALSE] Entering a motorway requires the acceleration lane; the deceleration lane is for leaving it.
[TRUE] The shoulder (banchina) is reserved for pedestrians and normally closed to vehicles.
[TRUE] The banchina is part of the road (strada), located outside the carriageway (carreggiata).
[TRUE] The banchina lies beyond the continuous white edge line (linea bianca continua di margine) of the carriageway.
[FALSE] The banchina is reserved for pedestrians; even slow vehicles uphill may not use it.
[FALSE] Parking (sosta) on the banchina is forbidden outright; there is no 5-hour allowance.
[FALSE] The banchina lies outside the carriageway and cannot divide it into lanes.
[FALSE] The banchina is not part of the carriageway and is not destined to parking.
[TRUE] The pavement (marciapiede) is a part of the road, raised or otherwise delimited, reserved for pedestrians.
[TRUE] The pavement is the part of the road normally reserved for pedestrians.
[TRUE] Vehicles may stop on a pavement only where specific parking markings (strisce di parcheggio) are present.
[TRUE] The pavement is the part of the road outside the carriageway destined to pedestrians.
[FALSE] The pavement is part of the road (strada) but lies outside the carriageway (carreggiata).
[FALSE] The pavement is reserved for pedestrians; bicycles must use the cycle path (pista ciclabile).
[FALSE] Parking on pavements is allowed only where parking bays are marked, regardless of whether it is raised.
[FALSE] Mopeds may not normally park on pavements; parking requires specific marked bays.
[TRUE] The pedestrian refuge (salvagente) at crossings shelters pedestrians and lets them pause midway while crossing.
[TRUE] The salvagente eases boarding and alighting of passengers from trams, trolleybuses and buses.
[TRUE] A salvagente may be signalled by bollards with fixed yellow lights (colonnine luminose a luce gialla fissa).
[FALSE] Separating traffic directions is the job of the central reservation (spartitraffico); the salvagente shelters crossing pedestrians.
[FALSE] Channelling vehicles is the function of the traffic island (isola di traffico); the salvagente protects pedestrians.
[FALSE] The salvagente is a fixed road feature sheltering pedestrians, not a first-aid person.
[FALSE] The salvagente is a refuge area for pedestrians, not a pedestrian-cycle route (itinerario ciclopedonale).
[TRUE] A driveway access (passo carrabile) lets vehicles enter private side areas such as garages or courtyards.
[TRUE] A passo carrabile must carry a specific sign showing the authorising body (ente) and the authorisation number.
[TRUE] The passo carrabile is the zone providing vehicle access to properties alongside the road.
[TRUE] At a passo carrabile a brief stop (fermata) is allowed, while parking (sosta) is forbidden.
[FALSE] A park-and-ride (parcheggio scambiatore) is unrelated; the passo carrabile is an access to private property.
[FALSE] The passo carrabile has nothing to do with animal-drawn carts; it is the access to private areas beside the road.
[FALSE] The passo carrabile is not a road reserved for trucks; it is the access to private properties alongside the road.
[FALSE] The passo carrabile is a vehicle access to private property, not a circular pedestrian refuge (salvagente).
[FALSE] The passo carrabile sign marks an access to private property; it does not impose roundabout circulation.
[FALSE] Parking (sosta) at a passo carrabile is forbidden; only a brief stop (fermata) is permitted.
[TRUE] A two-wheeled vehicle with a thermal engine up to 50 cm³ and a top speed of 45 km/h is a moped (ciclomotore).
[TRUE] Mopeds (ciclomotori) may have two or three wheels.
[TRUE] Not all two-wheeled motor vehicles are mopeds: those over 50 cm³ are motorcycles (motocicli).
[TRUE] A two-wheeled moped cannot have a thermal engine over 50 cm³; beyond that it is a motorcycle.
[TRUE] Mopeds must be inspected four years after first registration, then every two years (revisione).
[FALSE] Mopeds may also have three wheels, not just two.
[FALSE] Pedal-assisted bicycles with an auxiliary motor up to 0.25 kW are not classified as mopeds.
[FALSE] Two-wheelers over 50 cm³ are motorcycles (motocicli), not mopeds.
[FALSE] A manual gearbox is not required for a vehicle to be classed as a moped.
[FALSE] Mopeds are built for a maximum of 45 km/h, which applies everywhere, not only in town.
[FALSE] Mopeds are subject to periodic inspection (revisione): after four years, then every two years.
[TRUE] A motor tricycle (triciclo a motore) is a motor vehicle with three symmetrically arranged wheels.
[TRUE] Motor tricycles have engines over 50 cm³; three-wheelers up to 50 cm³ are mopeds.
[TRUE] Motor tricycles are inspected four years after first registration, then every two years.
[FALSE] Motor tricycles require a driving licence, like almost all motor vehicles.
[FALSE] A motorcycle plus sidecar is a motocarrozzetta with asymmetric wheels, not a triciclo a motore.
[FALSE] Motor tricycles are subject to periodic inspection (revisione).
[TRUE] Petrol-powered light quadricycles (quadricicli leggeri) have an engine capacity of no more than 50 cm³.
[TRUE] Quadricycles are motor vehicles with four wheels.
[TRUE] For circulation purposes light quadricycles are treated like mopeds (ciclomotori).
[TRUE] Quadricycles are subject to periodic inspection (revisione).
[FALSE] Non-light quadricycles require a B1 licence and a minimum age of 16.
[FALSE] Only light quadricycles are assimilated to mopeds; non-light ones are not.
[FALSE] It is forbidden to replace the exhaust or any part of a light quadricycle to raise its top speed.
[FALSE] Non-light quadricycles require age 16 and a B1 licence; at 14 (AM licence) only light ones may be driven.
[FALSE] Handlebar quadricycles with open bodywork (quads) require a helmet (casco).
[FALSE] Increasing the engine capacity of light quadricycles is forbidden.
[FALSE] Replacing the engine to exceed 45 km/h is forbidden; no modification may raise capacity or speed.
[FALSE] Quadricycles are subject to periodic inspection (revisione).
[TRUE] Registered agricultural machines may circulate on roads for their own transfer between sites.
[TRUE] Agricultural machines may be fitted with wheels or tracks (cingoli).
[TRUE] Wheeled or tracked agricultural machines may circulate to carry products and materials for agricultural and forestry businesses.
[TRUE] Agricultural machines may be self-propelled (semoventi) or towed (trainate).
[TRUE] Agricultural operating machines may carry special equipment for performing agricultural work.
[TRUE] Operating machines (macchine operatrici) may be self-propelled or towed.
[TRUE] Snowploughs (veicoli sgombraneve) are a typical example of operating machines.
